items.statement_summary: For any bifunctor F: I x J -> C such that the displayed limits and colimits exist, there is a canonical map kappa: colim_{i in I} lim_{j in J} F(i,j) -> lim_{j in J} colim_{i in I} F(i,j). The direction is dictated by colimits having a 'mapping out' and limits a 'mapping in' universal property. Proof: define components kappa_{i,j} as the composite of the limit-cone leg pi_{i,j}: lim_{j'} F(i,j') -> F(i,j) with the colimit-cone leg iota_{i,j}: F(i,j) -> colim_{i'} F(i',j); functoriality of F in both variables makes the kappa_{i,j} assemble into cones defining kappa_i and then kappa. Preceded by the general observation that limits commute with limits and colimits with colimits (Theorem 3.8.1 and its dual), while limits and colimits seldom commute with each other.

items.name: sup-inf is at most inf-sup
items.statement_summary: For any pair of sets X and Y and any function f: X x Y -> R, sup_{x in X} inf_{y in Y} f(x,y) <= inf_{y in Y} sup_{x in X} f(x,y), whenever these infima and suprema exist. Proof: specialize Lemma 3.8.3 to the poset category (R, <=), in which limits are infima and colimits suprema; the existence of the canonical map kappa: sup_X inf_Y f -> inf_Y sup_X f in that poset is exactly the displayed inequality.

items.name: the extended real line; lim inf and lim sup as iterated colimits and limits
items.statement_summary: Consider the extended real line R-bar := R union {-infinity, +infinity} with -infinity <= x <= +infinity for all real x. As a category it is complete and cocomplete: the limit of a function f: X -> R-bar is its infimum and the colimit its supremum, and these are the ordinary real numbers when the range of f is bounded - the point of working in R-bar being that boundedness hypotheses may be dropped and all limits and colimits exist. A function x: N -> R-bar is a sequence (x_n); regarding it as a bifunctor N x N -> N -> R-bar over the discrete category N x N, the LIM INF and LIM SUP are lim inf_n x_n = sup_{n>=0} inf_{m>=n} x_m = sup_{n>=0} inf_{m>=0} x_{n+m} = colim_n lim_m x_{n+m} and lim sup_n x_n = inf_{n>=0} sup_{m>=n} x_m = inf_{n>=0} sup_{m>=0} x_{n+m} = lim_n colim_m x_{n+m}. Lemma 3.8.3 then applies to give lim inf_n x_n <= lim sup_n x_n, and the limit of the sequence exists exactly when this inequality is an equality.

items.name: the analyst's proof of sup-inf <= inf-sup is the categorical one
items.statement_summary: The direct proof of Corollary 3.8.4 that would be given in a real analysis course is in fact the categorical proof of Lemma 3.8.3 unwound. Showing sup_X inf_Y f is bounded above by a quantity amounts, by the universal property of the supremum, to showing inf_Y f(x,-) is bounded above by it for each x in X; dually showing inf_Y sup_X f is bounded below by a quantity amounts to showing sup_X f(-,y) is bounded below by it for each y. So it suffices to prove inf_Y f(x,-) <= sup_X f(-,y) for each x and y, which follows by transitivity - i.e. composition - of inf_Y f(x,-) <= f(x,y) <= sup_X f(-,y).

items.name: filtered category
items.statement_summary: A category J is FILTERED if there is a cone under every FINITE diagram in J (finiteness in the sense of section 3.5: the indexing category has only finitely many morphisms). A footnote generalizes: replacing the smallest infinite cardinal omega by a regular cardinal kappa, a category is KAPPA-FILTERED if there is a cone under any diagram with fewer than kappa morphisms.

items.name: filtered and non-filtered categories
items.statement_summary: The category omega (and more generally any non-empty ordinal category) is filtered, as is the category with one object and one non-identity idempotent. The parallel pair category (two objects, two parallel non-identity arrows), the span category, and every discrete category other than the terminal category 1 are NOT filtered.

items.name: filtered colimits commute with finite limits in Set
items.statement_summary: Filtered colimits commute with finite limits in Set: for I a finite category, J a small filtered category and any functor F: I x J -> Set, the canonical map kappa: colim_{j in J} lim_{i in I} F(i,j) -> lim_{i in I} colim_{j in J} F(i,j) of Lemma 3.8.3 is a bijection. The proof rests on the explicit description of a filtered colimit in Set as the quotient of the coproduct in which x in F j and y in F k are identified precisely when there are maps f: j -> t and g: k -> t in J with F f(x) = F g(y); more generally any finite collection of elements identified in the colimit maps to a common element in some F t. Surjectivity: an element of the right-hand side is a cone with summit the singleton over the colimits; as I is finite it is given by finitely many elements satisfying finitely many compatibility conditions, and filteredness supplies a sufficiently large t in J at which they are simultaneously represented and assemble into a cone, i.e. an element of lim_i F(i,t). Injectivity: two elements of the left-hand side represented at j and k with a common image under kappa admit, for each i, some t_i identifying their components; finiteness of I plus filteredness of J gives a single t working for all i, so they already agree on the left. Riehl notes the proof is not categorical, but that in categories of models for an algebraic theory limits and filtered colimits are created in Set (Theorem 5.6.5), so finite limits and filtered colimits commute there as well.

items.name: idempotent splittings commute with all limits and colimits
items.statement_summary: Use the results of Exercise 3.4.vi to conclude that splittings of idempotents commute with both limits and colimits of any shape.

items.name: coprime group actions: BG-limits commute with BH-colimits
items.statement_summary: Show that if G and H are groups whose orders are coprime, then BG-indexed limits commute with BH-indexed colimits in Set. Reference [BJLS15] is given for more examples of this flavor.
